title: A term paper, written instead of an exam, gave us Huffman coding
body: In 1951, MIT professor Robert Fano gave his information theory students a choice: sit the final exam or write a paper on finding the most efficient binary code. David Huffman was about to give up when he hit on building the code from the bottom up, repeatedly pairing the two rarest symbols. Common symbols get short codes and rare ones long codes, and the result is provably the most efficient code of its kind. Variants still help compress ZIP files, JPEGs and MP3s.

slides.heading: Building a Huffman code, bottom up

steps.label: Count how often each symbol appears
Join the two rarest into one branch
Repeat until a single tree remains
Read codes off the branches: common = short

slides.question: What was Huffman’s key insight?
options: Pair the two rarest symbols, bottom up
Give every symbol the same length
Start from the most common symbol
slides.explanation: Huffman built the code from the bottom up, repeatedly pairing the two rarest symbols. Common symbols get short codes, rare ones long, and the result is provably the most efficient of its kind.

slides.heading: Which doesn’t rely on Huffman-style coding?
slides.explanation: ZIP, JPEG and MP3 all use Huffman-style codes to squeeze their data. A plain text file stores every character at full size, uncompressed.
